ranking.name: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center — services.swpc.noaa.gov
ranking.provides:
The operational space-weather feed. No key, no rate limit, updates every
1–5 minutes, and it carries both the raw measurements and the official
warnings:
* alerts.json — the actual issued Watches, Warnings and Alerts (geomagnetic
  storm G1–G5, radio blackout R1–R5, radiation storm S1–S5), with issue
  time and free-text product.
* noaa-scales.json — current and 3-day forecast R/S/G scale values.
* GOES X-ray flux (1-minute, 0.05–0.4 nm and 0.1–0.8 nm) — this is how you
  detect a solar flare and classify it A/B/C/M/X.
* GOES integral proton flux at >10/>50/>100 MeV — solar radiation storms,
  the thing that threatens astronauts, polar flights and satellite parts.
* GOES integral/differential electrons — surface and deep-dielectric
  charging risk for spacecraft.
* DSCOVR real-time solar wind at L1 (the /json/rtsw/ files; the older
  /products/solar-wind/ paths are gone) — density, speed, temperature and
  the interplanetary magnetic field including Bz, which is the single best
  ~30–60 minute lead indicator of a geomagnetic storm.
* Planetary K index (1-minute estimated and 3-hourly), Kp forecast.
* OVATION aurora nowcast grid, D-region absorption, 3-day forecast text.
* Solar-cycle indices: sunspot number and F10.7 monthly back to 1749.

endpoints.provides: product_id, issue_datetime, message (full NOAA alert text)

ranking.name: NASA CCMC DONKI (Space Weather Database of Notifications, Knowledge, Information)
ranking.org: NASA Goddard / Community Coordinated Modeling Center
ranking.provides:
Human-curated space-weather *events*, not raw instrument counts — which is
what you need to build a timeline or a causal chain. Separate endpoints per
event type: CME (time, source location, active region) and CME Analysis
(measured speed, half-angle, latitude/longitude, type S/C/O/R/ER plus the
WSA-ENLIL model run and its predicted Earth arrival time), solar flares
(begin/peak/end, class, active region, linked events), geomagnetic storms
(observed Kp series), solar energetic particle events, interplanetary
shocks, magnetopause crossings, radiation-belt enhancements, and the
notification texts themselves. Each event carries `linkedEvents`, so you
can trace flare -> CME -> shock -> storm as one chain.
Mirrored on api.nasa.gov (needs a key) and on the CCMC host (no key).

endpoints.provides: gstID, startTime, allKpIndex (observedTime, kpIndex, source), linkedEvents

endpoints.provides: messageType, messageID, messageIssueTime, messageBody

ranking.name: NASA/JPL Solar System Dynamics & CNEOS API
ranking.provides:
The authoritative machine-readable feed for asteroid and comet hazard.
Four distinct products behind one host:
* Close-Approach Data (CAD): every known close approach of an asteroid or
  comet to Earth (or any planet) between 1900 and 2200 — date, nominal and
  minimum distance in au / lunar distances, relative velocity, absolute
  magnitude H, and the 3-sigma uncertainty on time of approach.
* Sentry: the impact-risk table. Per object: number of potential impacts,
  impact probability, year range, Palermo and Torino scale ratings,
  estimated diameter and impact energy in megatons.
* Fireball: energy and location of atmospheric bolide detections by US
  government sensors since 1988 — date, lat/lon, altitude, velocity vector,
  total radiated energy and computed impact energy.
* SBDB / SBDB Query: full orbital elements, covariance, physical parameters
  (diameter, albedo, rotation, spectral type) and discovery circumstances
  for ~1.4M small bodies; the query endpoint does server-side filtering so
  you can pull "all PHAs with H < 22" in one request.

endpoints.provides: des, orbit_id, jd, cd, dist, dist_min, dist_max, v_rel, v_inf, t_sigma_f, h

endpoints.name: Impact-risk table (Palermo scale >= -5)
endpoints.provides: des, ip (impact probability), ps_cum, ts_max, diameter, energy, last_obs, n_imp

endpoints.name: Bolide / fireball detections
endpoints.provides: date, lat, lon, alt, vel, energy (kt), impact-e

endpoints.name: Bulk query — potentially hazardous asteroids
endpoints.provides: any of ~200 orbital/physical columns, server-side filtered

endpoints.name: Scout — imminent-impactor hazard assessment
endpoints.provides: impact probability and geographic corridor for objects still on the MPC confirmation page

ranking.name: CelesTrak
ranking.provides:
The keyless front door to the US catalogue of tracked objects, and the one
most projects actually build on:
* GP element sets for ~28,000 tracked objects in TLE, 3LE, JSON, CSV or OMM
  format, grouped (active, starlink, last-30-days, cosmos-2251-debris,
  iridium-33-debris, ...) or queried by NORAD ID / name. Feed these to an
  SGP4 propagator and you have every satellite and debris position.
* SATCAT — the object catalogue: international designator, launch date and
  site, object type, RCS size class, current orbital parameters, decay date
  for objects that have reentered, and operational status.
* SOCRATES — twice-daily all-on-all conjunction screening of the public
  catalogue: object pairs, time of closest approach, minimum range,
  relative velocity, maximum probability of collision.
* Space-weather CSV — historical and predicted Ap, Kp, F10.7 in exactly the
  form atmospheric-drag models want, which is what turns a TLE into a
  reentry-date estimate.

ranking.name: GFZ Potsdam geomagnetic indices (Kp / ap / Hp30 / Hp60)
ranking.org: GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences
ranking.provides:
The definitive Kp index — SWPC's Kp is an estimate, GFZ is the official
producer. The web service returns Kp and ap at 3-hour cadence continuously
from 1932, the international sunspot number and F10.7 on the same grid, and
the newer high-cadence Hp30/Hp60 and ap30/ap60 indices which resolve storm
substructure that 3-hourly Kp smears out. This is the series you use for
any statistical or historical study of geomagnetic risk, and the definitive
values that late-arriving corrections are applied to.

endpoints.provides: datetime array, Kp array, status (definitive/provisional)

endpoints.provides: full historical table, 3-hourly Kp and ap, daily Ap, sunspot number, F10.7

ranking.name: Helioviewer API
ranking.provides:
Programmatic access to the full solar-imagery archive — SDO/AIA and HMI,
SOHO/LASCO C2 and C3 coronagraphs, STEREO, PROBA-2, GOES/SUVI — from 1991
to now. You can ask for the closest image to a timestamp, build composite
layers, generate movies, and query the event layer. The LASCO coronagraph
frames are how a halo CME is actually recognised as Earth-directed before
any model runs, so this is the visual evidence layer behind a CME warning.

ranking.name: GCN — General Coordinates Network
ranking.provides:
The real-time alert bus for high-energy transients: gamma-ray bursts from
Swift and Fermi, gravitational-wave candidates from LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA,
high-energy neutrinos from IceCube, and magnetar giant flares. Notices
carry the trigger time, localisation (position plus error radius or a
HEALPix probability map), significance and classification, within seconds
to minutes of the event; Circulars are the human follow-up record going
back to 1997. Relevant to space hazards as the extreme tail — a nearby
magnetar giant flare or GRB is the only astrophysical event that ionises
Earth's atmosphere on human timescales — and as a source of realistic
event-driven alert plumbing.

endpoints.name: Circulars archive
endpoints.provides: circular number, subject, submitter, date, body (GRB/GW/neutrino follow-up reports)

ranking.name: NASA CDAWeb HAPI server
ranking.org: NASA Goddard Space Physics Data Facility
ranking.provides:
A standard HAPI (Heliophysics API) interface over roughly two thousand
space-physics datasets: OMNI merged solar wind at 1-minute and 1-hour
resolution back to 1963, ACE, Wind, DSCOVR, Cluster, THEMIS, Van Allen
Probes particle and field data, GOES energetic particles, and magnetometer
networks. Uniform request shape — /catalog, /info, /data with a time range
and parameter list — returns CSV or JSON. This is the archive-quality
counterpart to SWPC's real-time feed: worse latency, far better calibration
and depth, and the only practical way to get decades of L1 solar wind.

endpoints.provides: dataset ids and titles for every available collection

endpoints.provides: time, Dst (and ~50 more parameters on request; HAPI requires them in dataset order)

ranking.name: NEODyS-2
ranking.provides:
The third independent impact-monitoring system (the original CLOMON2 line
of work). Per NEO it publishes orbital elements with full covariance, the
observation arc, residuals, ephemerides, close-approach tables, and the
risk page listing virtual impactors with date, impact probability, Palermo
and Torino values. Also serves the raw astrometric observation files, which
lets you re-fit an orbit yourself rather than trusting a published one.

endpoints.provides: designation, date, impact probability, Palermo, Torino, H, diameter

ranking.name: SILSO — World Data Center for the Sunspot Index
ranking.provides:
The official international sunspot number — the longest continuous record
of solar activity, daily since 1818 and monthly since 1749, plus the
13-month smoothed series, hemispheric split, the estimated (provisional)
current-month value updated daily, and the official solar-cycle prediction.
Sunspot number is the baseline against which "is this cycle dangerous"
questions are answered, and it drives thermospheric-density models that
determine satellite drag and debris lifetime.

endpoints.provides: year, month, day, decimal date, estimated SN, std dev, n stations

endpoints.name: Daily total sunspot number since 1818
endpoints.provides: date, daily SN, standard deviation, observations, definitive/provisional flag

probes.name: Estimated international sunspot number, current month

ranking.name: American Meteor Society fireball reports
ranking.license: Free API key for non-commercial use
ranking.provides:
Crowd-sourced fireball sightings, usually within minutes of an event and
often before any official detection is published. Each event aggregates
eyewitness reports into a computed trajectory: start and end lat/lon and
altitude, ground track, velocity, estimated magnitude, sound and
fragmentation reports, and the individual report records. This is the
fastest public signal that something just entered the atmosphere over a
populated area, and it covers events too small for CNEOS sensors.

ranking.name: Global Meteor Network
ranking.provides:
A worldwide network of low-cost video meteor cameras publishing fully
reduced, open trajectory data nightly: per-meteor radiant, geocentric and
heliocentric velocity, orbital elements, absolute magnitude, mass estimate,
begin and end height, and the observing stations that saw it. Aggregated
daily and monthly files plus a live fireball page. It is the only open
dataset that quantifies the small-impactor flux — the population between
"harmless meteor" and "CNEOS-detectable bolide" — which is what a
statistical risk model for small impacts needs.

endpoints.name: Monthly trajectory summary files
endpoints.provides: index of monthly CSVs with per-meteor orbits, radiants, velocities, magnitudes, masses

ranking.name: Heliophysics Event Knowledgebase (HEK)
ranking.org: Lockheed Martin Solar & Astrophysics Lab / NASA
ranking.provides:
A searchable database of automatically and manually detected solar features
and events across all major solar observatories: flares, filament
eruptions, coronal holes, sigmoids, sunspots, emerging flux, CMEs and
coronal dimmings. Each record carries start/peak/end times, heliographic
bounding box and chain code, the detection algorithm, the instrument, GOES
class where applicable, and links to the source data. Coronal-hole records
are the practical way to anticipate recurrent high-speed-stream storms
that have no flare or CME attached to them.

endpoints.name: Flare events from the HEK query interface
endpoints.provides: event_starttime, event_peaktime, fl_goescls, ar_noaanum, frm_name, obs_instrument

probes.name: Flare events from the HEK query interface

ranking.name: LASP Interactive Solar Irradiance Data Center (LISIRD)
ranking.provides:
Solar irradiance and solar-index time series served through the LaTiS API:
total solar irradiance composites back to 1978 and reconstructions back to
1610, spectral irradiance from SORCE/TSIS, the Mg II core-to-wing index,
and the adjusted and observed F10.7 radio flux from Penticton. F10.7 is the
standard driver of every operational thermosphere-density model, so this
feeds directly into satellite-drag and reentry-timing estimates.

endpoints.name: Penticton F10.7 solar radio flux
endpoints.provides: time, adjusted_flux, observed_flux (10.7 cm, sfu)

ranking.name: Space-Track.org
ranking.org: US Space Force / 18th & 19th Space Defense Squadron
ranking.license: Free account, redistribution restricted by user agreement
ranking.provides:
The authoritative upstream. A free account unlocks data that exists
nowhere else: the full GP and GP_HISTORY element catalogue including
analyst objects, CDM_PUBLIC conjunction data messages for operators
(miss distance, collision probability, covariance at TCA), the DECAY
table and Tracking and Impact Prediction (TIP) messages giving predicted
reentry time and ground footprint with an uncertainty window, boxscore
statistics per country, and SATCAT change logs. Everything CelesTrak
publishes is derived from here, minus the CDMs and TIPs.
Access is by POST login to /ajaxauth/login followed by REST queries; the
user agreement forbids bulk redistribution, so treat it as a private feed.

endpoints.name: Service liveness (unauthenticated login endpoint)
endpoints.provides: confirms the API host is reachable; real queries require credentials

ranking.name: IAU Minor Planet Center
ranking.provides:
The single clearing house every other NEO product depends on: it receives
raw astrometry from the world's telescopes, assigns designations, and
publishes the orbit catalogue. For hazard work the important products are
the NEA orbit files (orbital elements, H, arc length, number of oppositions,
MOID), the NEO Confirmation Page listing brand-new unconfirmed objects that
may be on an impacting trajectory, the daily orbit-update files, and the
raw observation records in the ADES/obs80 formats. If an object is not here
yet, no risk system knows about it.

endpoints.provides: temporary designation, discovery date, RA/Dec, V magnitude, motion, NEO score, n_obs

ranking.name: NASA NeoWs (Near Earth Object Web Service)
ranking.provides:
A friendlier re-packaging of JPL SBDB/CAD keyed by date: "what passes close
to Earth this week". Per object it returns estimated diameter min/max in
four unit systems, the is_potentially_hazardous_asteroid flag, close-approach
date, relative velocity, miss distance, the orbiting body, plus a browse
endpoint over the whole ~40k NEO catalogue. Easier to consume than the raw
JPL APIs but derived from them, rate-limited, and needs a key.

endpoints.provides: total NEO count, total close-approach count, last updated, source

ranking.name: USGS Earthquake Catalog (FDSN event service)
ranking.provides:
Seismic and infrasound-adjacent event records with origin time, location,
depth, magnitude and magnitude type, in GeoJSON. Large bolide airbursts
register on seismic and infrasound networks, so this is a cross-check for
confirming and geolocating an atmospheric impact independently of optical
reports — the Chelyabinsk airburst appears in seismic records. Also the
cleanest public example of an FDSN-standard query interface.

endpoints.name: Recent significant events
endpoints.provides: time, place, mag, magType, depth, coordinates, event type, felt reports

ranking.name: NASA Satellite Situation Center (SSCWeb)
ranking.org: NASA Goddard Space Physics Data Facility
ranking.provides:
Where a spacecraft is relative to the magnetosphere, not just relative to
Earth: positions for hundreds of heliophysics missions in GEO, GSE, GSM and
SM coordinates, plus magnetic-field-line tracing and region classification
(magnetosheath, magnetotail, plasmasphere, radiation belt, bow shock and
magnetopause crossings). For radiation-exposure and charging questions the
magnetospheric region matters more than the altitude, and this is the only
service that resolves it.

endpoints.name: Available observatories
endpoints.provides: spacecraft id, name, resolution, start and end time of available ephemeris

ranking.name: NASA/JPL Horizons ephemeris API
ranking.provides:
Numerically integrated ephemerides for any solar-system body, spacecraft or
user-supplied orbit, as seen from any observing site. Used for turning a
hazard catalogue entry into an actual sky position, range and range-rate:
RA/Dec, apparent magnitude, Earth and Sun distance, phase angle, elongation,
illumination, and state vectors in a chosen reference frame at arbitrary
time steps. This is the ground truth other NEO products are checked against.

endpoints.name: Observer table for 99942 Apophis
endpoints.provides: date, RA, Dec, apparent magnitude, delta (Earth range), deldot, S-O-T elongation

ranking.name: HEASARC Virtual Observatory TAP service
ranking.org: NASA Goddard High Energy Astrophysics Science Archive
ranking.provides:
ADQL/SQL access over hundreds of high-energy mission catalogues — the Swift
and Fermi GRB tables, all-sky monitor light curves, source catalogues and
observation logs. For hazard work it is the archive that turns a transient
alert into a historical rate: how often a burst of a given fluence occurs,
with what sky distribution. Standard IVOA TAP, so any VO client or a plain
HTTP GET with a query string works.

endpoints.provides: table names and column metadata for every HEASARC catalogue

Europe's independent impact-monitoring chain (AstOD/Aegis), computed
separately from Sentry — valuable precisely because it is an independent
check on JPL. Downloadable flat files give the Risk List (objects with a
non-zero impact probability: designation, year range, impact probability,
Palermo scale, diameter, velocity), the Priority List telling observers
which objects urgently need follow-up astrometry, the Close Approaches
list, and per-object orbital elements and observation arcs.

ranking.name: GCAT — Jonathan McDowell's General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects
ranking.provides:
A hand-curated, heavily cross-checked catalogue of everything launched
since 1957 — objects, launches, launch vehicles, sites, organisations,
reentries and deep-space probes — with the historical corrections and
identity resolutions the official catalogues never made. It is the best
source for provenance questions ("what object actually was this", "when
did it really reenter", "which launch did this fragment come from") and
for reentry statistics over the whole space age. Plain tab-delimited
tables, trivially parsable.

ranking.name: NASA EONET (Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker)
ranking.provides:
A curated GeoJSON feed of ongoing natural events observed from orbit —
wildfires, severe storms, volcanoes, dust and haze, icebergs, landslides.
Not a space hazard itself, but the standard way to correlate a candidate
space-related signature with a mundane terrestrial explanation, and a
clean reference implementation of an event/category/geometry API.

endpoints.name: Open events
endpoints.provides: event id, title, category, sources, geometry (point or polygon) with date

ranking.name: ESA DISCOSweb
ranking.provides:
Europe's Database and Information System Characterising Objects in Space:
the physical-properties catalogue that the US catalogue lacks. Per object
it gives mass, dimensions (span, height, depth), cross-section (minimum,
maximum and average), shape, and construction materials; plus launch
records, reentry epochs, fragmentation events with cause and resulting
debris counts, and destination orbits. Mass and area are exactly what you
need to convert "an object is reentering" into "how much survives to the
ground" or to compute an area-to-mass ratio for drag. JSON:API over HTTPS
with a bearer token.

ranking.name: Where the ISS at? API
ranking.provides:
Instant SGP4-propagated position, velocity, altitude, footprint, solar
illumination and ground-track lat/lon for any catalogued satellite by NORAD
ID, plus TLE retrieval and timestamp-batch queries. No key, no rate limit
worth worrying about. Useful as a zero-setup positional layer or a sanity
check on your own propagator, but it is derived from public TLEs and adds
no independent information.

endpoints.name: ISS position now
endpoints.provides: latitude, longitude, altitude, velocity, visibility, footprint, solar_lat, solar_lon, daynum

ranking.name: Aerospace Corporation CORDS reentry predictions
ranking.provides:
NOTE: verified as NOT programmatically accessible — the site sits behind a
WAF that answers automated requests with HTTP 403 and a challenge page.
Read it in a browser; do not plan a scraper around it. Its probe is left
in place and left failing so the ranking reflects that.

Independent, publicly readable reentry predictions for large uncontrolled
objects: predicted reentry time with an uncertainty window, ground-track
maps for the possible reentry passes, object mass and expected surviving
debris, and post-event reconstructions. Where Space-Track's TIP messages
are terse and access-controlled, CORDS is the public narrative layer,
updated as the prediction tightens in the final days.

endpoints.name: Reentry predictions index
endpoints.provides: object name, NORAD ID, predicted reentry window, uncertainty, status
